management: TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITALr Airway must be vigilantly monitored: – Edema or expanding hematoma can progress to airway compromise. r Orotracheal intubation preferred 1st-line technique for airway control r Clinical signs of respiratory distress: – Stridor – Air hunger – Labored breathing – Expanding neck hematoma r Blind nasotracheal intubation should be avoided: – Owing to anatomy distortion and risk of hematoma rupture r Cervical spine must be stabilized. Rosen BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Pericardial effusion: – Pericardial sac usually contains 15–40 cc of fluid – Collection of additional fluid = effusion r Pericardial tamponade: – Accumulation of pericardial fluid causes an elevation of pressure in the pericardial space, resulting in impairment of ventricular filling and decreased cardiac output. – Depends on size and speed of fluid accumulation – Increase of as little as 80–120 cc of fluid may lead to a rise in pericardial pressure. – Up to 70% present in “early tamponade” and appear clinically stable – Occurs in 2% of patients with penetrating chest trauma ETIOLOGYr Medical causes: – Pericarditis (20%): ◦90% idiopathic or viral ◦Bacterial, fungal, parasitic, tuberculosis, HIV – Malignancy (13%): ◦Lymphoma, leukemia, melanoma, breast, lung ◦Metastatic disease, primary malignancy, postradiation – Postmyocardial infarction (8%): ◦Acute: 1–3 days after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) ◦Subacute (Dressler syndrome): Weeks to months after AMI ◦Incidence reduced with reperfusion therapy – End-stage renal disease, uremia (6%) – Autoimmune/collagen vascular disease (5%): Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma – Rheumatic fever – Radiation therapy – Myxed

highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch424.xml May 16, 2014 17:1 PERTUSSIS Adam Z. Barkin BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Acute respiratory tract infection spread by small respiratory droplets r Bacteria (fimbriae) attach to respiratory epithelial cells and proliferate, producing toxins: – Ciliary dysfunction, accumulation of cellular debris, increased mucus production, lymphocytic and granulocytic infiltration r Bronchiolar congestion, obstruction, and necrosis r Obstruction of the airway due to mucus plug, leading to hypoxia and hypoventilation r Increased intrathoracic or intracranial pressure r Secondary bacterial infection may exacerbate respiratory distress/failure. r CNS injury caused by encephalitis, increased intracranial pressure, and/or hypoxia r Uncomplicated cases last 6–10 wk; half of the cases last <6 wk. r Mortality: – Mortality greatest in those <1y r – 1.3% for patients <1m o – 0.3% in children 2–11 mo – 90% of deaths are secondary to bacterial pneumonia r Epidemiology: – Incubation period is 6–20 days, usually 7–10 days. – Mostly young children; 24% in children <6m o – Increasing incidence in adolescents – Adults are the primary reservoir – Peak incidence is late summer/fall – Preventable with diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis (Tdap) vaccine ETIOLOGY Bordetella pertussis: r A fastidious, gram-negative, pleomorphic bacillus DIAGNOSIS
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Generally 3 recognized phases with progression: – Infants may have indistinct stages r Catarrhal stage: – 1–2 wk duration – Rhinorrhea – Mild cough – Minimal fever r Paroxysmal stage: – 1–6 wk duration – Classic “whooping” cough, increasing in severity: ◦Coughing spasm that ends with a sudden inflow of air—the whoop; unremitting paroxysms – Cyanosis with respiratory distress/failure – Apnea (infants <6 mo) – Altered mental status secondary to hypoxia or encephalitis r Convalescent stage: – 2–12 wk duration – Waning cough – Improving respiratory status r Atypical presentations: – Often atypical in children <6m o – Partially immunized children have less severe disease – Adult manifestations are often only rhinorrhea, sore throat, persistent cough; often in family members Historyr Catarrhal phase: – Malaise – Low-grade fever – Rhinorrhea – Sore throat r Paroxysmal phase: – “Whooping” cough – Post-tussive cyanosis – Post-tussive emesis r “Whooping” sound during paroxys
management: TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITALr Oxygen r Monitor airway r Suction INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Oxygen and respiratory support r Suction mucous plugs ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Universal precautions: – Specifically requires droplet precautions for 5 days after initiation of antimicrobial therapy r Maintenance of adequate hydration r Monitor oxygenation during paroxysms; supplement oxygen r Airway management may be lifesaving in younger children r Antibiotics: – Effective in the catarrhal stage – Prevent further transmission in the paroxysmal stage – Azithromycin is the first-line agent – Alternatively, clarithromycin, erythromycin, or trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole may be used, although the efficacy is unproven; useful if erythromycin is not tolerated r Corticosteroids and albuterol may reduce paroxysms of coughing, but further studies are required r With increasing incidence of pertussis among adolescents and adults, emergency physicians can decrease incidence of pertussis by making vaccination routine

highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch430.xml May 16, 2014 17:1 PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA David N. Zull BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Pheochromocytoma (pheo) is a catecholamine- producing tumor arising from the chromaffin tissues of the sympathetic nervous system. r Origin from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia: – 80% solitary adrenal (usually the right side) – 10% bilateral (usually inherited form) – 10% extra-adrenal in location: ◦Abdominal, within mesenteric ganglia (86%) ◦Thorax (10%), neck (3%), bladder (1%) – 10% malignant (usually inherited form) r Incidence: – 0.2–0.4% of hypertensive patients, but higher proportion of patients with severe hypertension – 2–8/million population per year – Peaks in decades 3–5, 10% in children – Male = female – In about 1/2 of the cases, the diagnosis is made postmortem. – 10% asymptomatic, incidental on CT r Genetics: – Inherited form 25%, autosomal dominant – Usually associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 2A, less so with MEN 2B or von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease: ◦MEN 2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma [CA], pheo, and hyperparathyroidism) ◦MEN 2B (medullary thyroid CA, pheo, oral mucosal neuromas, skeletal and bony abnormalities) ◦VHL (hemangioblastomas of retina and CNS, pancreas and renal cysts, and pheo – Other associated diseases: Neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge–Weber syndrom

highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch431.xml May 16, 2014 17:1 PHIMOSIS Nicole M. Franks BASICS DESCRIPTIONr True phimosis is the pathologic inability to retract the foreskin over the glans of the penis as a result of scarring. r The inability to retract a normal, supple foreskin is not true phimosis. r The foreskin is rarely retractable at birth due to normal adhesions between the glans and the inner prepuce. r ∼90% are retractable by 3 yr of age, and 99% are retractable by 17 yr, as the epithelial cells that comprise smegma are shed. r Parents should be instructed not to forcibly retract the foreskin. diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Dysuria, hematuria r Poor urinary stream r Whitish, narrowed preputial opening of the foreskin r Edema, erythema, and tenderness of prepuce r Balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans and foreskin) r Ballooning of foreskin on urination in severe cases Physical Exam Exam should include an evaluation for potential complications: r Obstruction and vascular compromise of glans r Occur only in the most extreme cases ESSENTIAL WORKUPr In the majority of cases, no workup is necessary. r In patients with severe stenosis, the complication of an obstructive uropathy may occur. This should be investigated by: – Evaluation of kidney function: ◦BUN and creatinine – Renal sonogram r Phimosis secondary to recurrent balanoposthitis should prompt a workup for diabetes mellitus: – Urinalysis, serum glucose, or glycosylated hemoglobin (Hgb A1C) DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Preputial adhesions are normal in young children. r Balanoposthitis without phimosis TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITALr Pre-hos
management: TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITALr Pre-hospital personnel and family members should be instructed not to attempt retraction of the foreskin prior to medical evaluation. r Unwarranted attempts may traumatize a normal, nonretractable prepuce or convert the situation to a more emergent paraphimosis. INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY None required in most cases 862 P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch431.xml May 16, 2014 17:1 PHIMOSIS P ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Relieve obstructive uropathy, if present, with urethral catheterization or suprapubic aspiration. r If vascular flow to the glans is compromised, a dorsal slit must be made in the foreskin: – Performed after achieving adequate penile block (see Paraphimosis for more detailed description of procedure) – This is rarely necessary in phimosis. r Potent topical steroids for a multiweek course have been reported to successfully reduce phimosis: – Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05–0.1%: Apply to preputial orifice twice

highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch435.xml May 16, 2014 17:1 PLEURAL EFFUSION Sierra Beck rSteven M. Lindsey BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Normal conditions: – Pleural space contains 0.1–0.2 mL/kg (30 mL in an adult) of clear, low-protein fluid that facilitates movement of the pulmonary parenchyma within the thoracic space. – Fluid formation and reabsorption are governed by hydrostatic and oncotic forces. – Normally, the sum of these forces results in movement of fluid into the pleural space from the parietal surface and reabsorption at the visceral surface. – Lymphatics help remove any excess fluid. r Alteration of any of the above factors results in abnormal fluid accumulation. r Classification: – Transudative effusion: ◦An ultrafiltrate of serum, containing low protein and cells ◦Results from increase in hydrostatic pressure and/or decrease in oncotic pressure ◦Pleural surface is not involved in the primary pathologic process. – Exudative effusion: ◦Contains high protein and cells ◦Results from pathologic disease of the pleural surface leading to membrane permeability and/or disruption of lymphatic reabsorption ETIOLOGYr Transudative effusions: – Congestive heart failure (CHF) – Peritoneal dialysis – Cirrhosis with ascites – Pulmonary embolism – Acute atelectasis – Nephrotic syndrome – Myxedema – Hypoproteinemia – Superior vena cava syndr
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Small effusions are often asymptomatic. r Dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and/or cough r Tachypnea, hypoxia, decreased breath sounds, and/or dullness to percussion Historyr Underlying primary pathologic process (CHF , pneumonia, pulmonary embolus, pancreatitis) is often the source of complaints. r Dyspnea on exertion or at rest r Cough with large effusion r Pleuritic chest pain with inflammation of pleura r Empyema: Fever, fatigue, weight loss Physical Examr Decreased breath sounds r Decreased tactile fremitus r Increased egophony for large effusions r Dullness to chest percussion r Pleural friction rub r Examine for the primary cause of pleural effusion. highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-P LWBK1336-Schaider ch440.xml May 23, 2014 14:22 PNEUMOTHORAX William Porcaro BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Presence of free air in the intrapleural space r Spontaneous pneumothorax is due to atraumatic rupture of alveolus, bronchiole, or bleb. r Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (2/3 of incidences): – No underlying pulmonary pathology present – Rupture of small subpleural cyst or bleb – Primarily young, healthy patients (20–40 yr old) with tall, thin body habitus – Risk factors: Smoking, family history, Marfan syndrome, homocystinuria, thoracic endometriosis r Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from underlying pulmonary pathology (see Etiology) r Tension pneumothorax: – Air continues to enter pleural space through bronchoalveolar disruption and becomes trapped via “ball-valve” mechanism. – Intrapleural pressure increases. – Venous return to right heart decreases, resulting in decrease in cardiac output. – Mediastinum shifts toward uninvolved side, mechanically interfering with right atrial filling. – Ventilation compromise and ventilation/perfusion mismatch result in hypoxemia ETIOLOGYr Idiopathic r Airway disease: – Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – Asthma – Cystic fibrosis r Infections: – Necrotizing bacterial pneumonia –T B – Fungal pneumonia – Pneumocystis carinii r Neoplasm r Interstitial lung disease: – Sarcoi
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr Severity of symptoms is generally proportional to size of the pneumothorax. r Chest pain on the ipsilateral side: – Sharp, pleuritic pain – Sudden onset – Dull ache in delayed presentations r Shortness of breath r Rarely cough, asymptomatic, or generalized malaise Physical Examr Tachypnea r Heart rate <120 bpm generally seen in simple spontaneous pneumothoraces r Jugular venous distention and tracheal deviation to the contralateral side may be evident in tension pneumothorax. r Cardiac and pulmonary exam: – Asymmetric decreased breath sounds – Hyperresonance to percussion of ipsilateral side r Tension pneumothorax: – Hypotension – Tachycardia, heart rate>120 bpm – Diaphoresis – Cyanosis – Cardiovascular collapse – Tracheal deviation ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Imaging is mainstay of the workup r DO NOT delay chest decompression if the patient is hemodynamically unstable and there is sufficient clinical evidence of pneumothorax. highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-R LWBK1336-Schaider ch469.xml May 16, 2014 20:51 RABIES Herbert Neil Wigder r Ashley Alwood r Matthew A. Kippenhand BASICS DESCRIPTION CNS infectious disease of mammals caused by the rabies virus: r Highest case fatality rate of any known infectious disease ETIOLOGYr Epidemiology: – 30,000–70,000 people die/yr worldwide – Especially common in Southeast Asia, Philippines, Africa, South America, and Indian subcontinent – US has 2–3 human cases per year. – Most clinical cases in US from foreign travel and bat exposures – Raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats, dogs, woodchucks, groundhogs are reservoirs. – In US bats are the most common reservoir while abroad dogs are more common. – Squirrels, rats, mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, gerbils, chipmunks, and rabbits can also be infected but there has never been a reported case of human transmission. r Pathophysiology: – Negative-stranded RNA genome, family Rhabdoviridae, genus Lyssavirus – Mode of transmission: ◦Contact with infected saliva of host ◦Bite: Most common ◦Nonbite: Saliva or bat aerosol exposure to an open wound or mucous membrane ◦Transplant procedures are the only well-documented person-to-person transmission ◦Not considered a transmission risk: Petting rabid animal or contact with the blood, urine, or feces of a rabid animal – Progression after infection: ◦Virus multiplies
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Once a patient exhibits clinical signs course is almost universally fatal. r 5 stages: Incubation, prodrome, encephalitis, coma, death (or recovery): – Incubation: 1–3 mo (range 10 days to 1 yr): ◦Virus amplifies in peripheral tissues ◦Time depends on amount inoculated and proximity to CNS, thus shorter incubation for head or neck bites – Prodrome: 1–7 days: ◦Nonspecific symptoms: Fever, headache, malaise, myalgias, anorexia, sore throat, nausea, and vomiting ◦Paresthesias or fasciculations around bite site give clue to diagnosis. – Encephalitis (classic form): 2–7 days: ◦Anxiety, agitation, hallucinations, confusion or delirium, muscle spasms, opisthotonos, and seizure ◦Aerophobia (pathognomonic): Pharyngeal spasm from draft of air ◦Hydrophobia (pathognomonic): Violent involuntary muscle contraction of diaphragm, pharyngeal, laryngeal, and accessory respiratory muscles when attempting to swallow (seen in up to half of cases) ◦Dysrhythmias, myocarditis, autonomic i

chapters.title: RENAL CALCULUS
highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-R LWBK1336-Schaider ch476.xml May 16, 2014 17:17 RENAL CALCULUS Matthew A. Wheatley rRyan A. Stroder BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Urinary tract obstruction r Intermittent distention of the renal pelvis of proximal ureter produces pain r Kidney stones: – Most common cause of renal colic – Stone composition: ◦80%: Calcium stones (calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate) ◦5% uric acid ◦Others: Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite), cystine – Associated with infections caused by urea-splitting organisms (e.g., Pseudomonas, Proteus, Klebsiella) along with an alkalotic urine – 90% of urinary calculi are radiopaque ETIOLOGYr 6–12% lifetime risk in the general population r Twice as common in men as women r Peak incidence between 40 and 60 yr old r Theories on stone formation: – Urinary supersaturation of solute followed by crystal precipitation – Decrease in the normal urinary proteins inhibiting crystal growth – Urinary stasis from a physical anomaly, catheter placement, neurogenic bladder, or the presence of a foreign body r Recurrence rate of 40% at 5 yr and 75% at 20 yr r Associated with chronic kidney disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, metabolic syndrome, and an increased risk of coronary artery disease Pediatric Considerations r Rare in children r When present, often is an indication of a metabolic or genetic disorder
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr Sudden onset of severe pain in the costovertebral angle, flank, and/or lateral abdomen r Colicky or constant pain: – Patient cannot find a comfortable position r Hematuria: – Gross hematuria in 1/3 of patients r Nausea/vomiting r Diaphoresis r History of prior stone formation Physical Examr Vital signs: – Fever suggests an occult infection. – Hypotension with an altered mental status suggests urosepsis r Abdominal exam: – Tenderness to palpation, rebound tenderness, or guarding suggests a more serious intra-abdominal process – Palpate the abdominal aorta for tenderness or pulsatile enlargement suggestive of an aneurysm r Genitourinary exam: – Examine the genitalia for evidence of hernia, epididymitis, torsion, or testicular masses ESSENTIAL WORKUPr Urinalysis – Microscopic hematuria present in >80% – Gross hematuria – Absent urinary blood in 10–30% – WBC/bacteria suggests infection – No correlation between the amount of hematuria and the degree of urinary o
management: TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITAL Parenteral opiates may be required for pain control with long transport times INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPYr Rapid dipstick urine test for blood: – Positive test in conjunction with clinical findings sufficient to begin analgesic therapy r Provide adequate analgesia when diagnosis suspected on clinical and lab findings ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Hydration: – Initiate IV crystalloid infusion with 1 L of normal saline infused over 30–60 min followed by 200–500 mL/h – Bolus volume compromised patients with 500 mL increments until urine output adequate r Analgesics (morphine, ketorolac): – Combination of IV NSAIDs and opioids decrease ED stay and provide better pain control than either alone r Antiemetics (prochlorperazine, ondansetron, droperidol, hydroxyzine) r α-Blockers (tamsulosin) or calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine) have been shown to decrease time to spontaneous stone passage: – Most efficacious for stones <5 mm in diameter – Tamsulosin and nifedipine equally effect

Graber BASICS DESCRIPTIONr The disorder is now known as acute kidney injury (AKI); the term renal failure is outdated. r Changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and urine output (UO) encompassing a spectrum ranging from normal physiologic response to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and measured by accumulation of nitrogenous by-products. r Defined by the RIFLE criteria: – 3 stages of renal injury: ◦Risk: Increased creatinine (Cr) ×1.5 or GFR decrease >25%, UO <0.5 mL/kg/h × >6h ◦Injury: Increased Cr ×2 or GFR decrease >50%, UO <0.5 mL/kg/h × >12 h ◦Failure: Increased Cr ×3 or GFR decrease >75% or Cr ≥4 mg/dL (acute rise of ≥0.5 mg/dL), UO <0.3 mL/kg/h × 2 4ho r anuria × 12 h – 2 stages of outcome: ◦Loss: Loss of renal function >4w k ◦ESRD: Loss of renal function >3m o r The most severe marker defines stage. r AKI based upon changes within last 48h; however, must often base on most recent data. r Higher RIFLE stages correlate with higher 1 and 6 mo mortality rates for hospitalized patients. ETIOLOGYr Prerenal AKI: – Caused by renal hypoperfusion – Renal tissue remains normal unless severe/prolonged hypoperfusion. r Intrarenal AKI: – Caused by diseases of the renal parenchyma r Iatrogenic AKI causes include

chapters.title: RENAL INJURY
highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-R LWBK1336-Schaider ch478.xml May 16, 2014 17:17 RENAL INJURY Albert S. Jin BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Kidneys are located in the retroperitoneal space and are surrounded by adipose tissue and loose areolar connective tissue. r Kidneys lie along the lower 2 thoracic vertebrae and 1st 4 lumbar vertebrae. r Left kidney is positioned slightly higher than the right. r Kidneys are not fixed: – Shift with the diaphragm and are supported by the renal arteries, veins, and adipose tissue to the renal (Gerota) fascia ETIOLOGYr Most common of all urologic injuries r Occurs in ∼8–10% of all abdominal trauma r Blunt renal trauma accounts for 80–85% of all renal injuries and is 5 times more common than penetrating injury: – Mechanisms include motor vehicle accidents, falls, domestic violence, and contact sports. – Pathophysiology includes rapid deceleration and displacement mechanisms. – ∼20% of cases are associated with intraperitoneal injury. r Mechanisms responsible for significant renal injury almost never affect the kidney alone: – Most often disrupt and injure other vital organs that can be responsible for patient mortality r Renal injuries are graded by type and severity of injury (Association for the Surgery of Trauma [AAST] criteria) – Grade I ◦Contusion: Microscopic or gross hematuria, urologic studies normal ◦Hematoma: Subcapsul
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr Mechanism of injury and kinematics are important factors. r Majority of renal injuries are associated with injury of other abdominal organs. r In blunt trauma, note the type and direction (horizontal or vertical) of any deceleration or compressive forces. r In penetrating trauma, note the characteristic of the weapon (type and caliber), distance from the weapon, or the type and length of knife or impaling object: – Injuries result from a combination of kinetic energy and shear forces of penetrating object. management: treatment of blunt renal trauma: – Major renal lacerations represent significant reparable renal injuries. – Adult patients at risk for having sustained major lacerations: ◦Gross hematuria, or ◦Microhematuria (≥3–5 RBCs/HPF) with shock (systolic BP ≤90 mm Hg) in the field or on arrival in the ED, or ◦History of sudden deceleration without hematuria or shock r IV contrast-enhanced CT scan is the procedure of choice in identifying urologic injury. r Guidelines are not applicable in cases of penetrating renal trauma or in children. r Adults with blunt renal trauma and gross hematuria, or microhematuria in the presence of shock, require renal imaging for further evaluation of renal injury. r In adults with penetrating renal trauma, significant injuries to the kidney and ureter can occur without hematuria: – Location of penetrating wound in relation to urinary tract is the most important factor in deciding need for radiographic imaging. – Penetrating injuries with any degree of hematuria should be i

Jin BASICS DESCRIPTIONr The spleen is formed by reticular and lymphatic tissue and is the largest lymph organ. r The spleen lies posterolaterally in the left upper quadrant (LUQ) between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm. ETIOLOGYr The spleen is the most commonly injured intra-abdominal organ: – In nearly 2/3 of cases, it is the only damaged intraperitoneal structure – Blunt mechanisms are more common r Motor vehicle accidents (auto–auto, pedestrian–auto) are the major cause (50–75%), followed by blows to the abdomen (15%) and falls (6–9%) r Mechanism of injury and kinematics are important factors in evaluating patients for possible splenic injury. r Splenic injuries are graded by type and severity of injury [American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) criteria]: – Grade I: ◦Hematoma: Subcapsular,<10% surface area ◦Laceration: Capsular tear,<1c mi n parenchymal depth – Grade II: ◦Hematoma: Subcapsular, 10–50% surface area; intraparenchymal, <5 cm in diameter ◦Laceration: Capsular tear, 1–3 cm in parenchymal depth and not involving a trabecular vessel – Grade III: ◦Hematoma: Subcapsular,>50% surface area or expanding, ruptured subcapsular or parenchymal hematoma; intraparenchymal hematoma, ≥5 cm or expanding ◦Laceration: >3 cm i
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr In blunt trauma, note the type and direction (horizontal or vertical) of any deceleration or compressive forces: – Injuries are caused by compression of the spleen between the anterior abdominal wall and the posterior thoracic cage or vertebra (e.g., lap-belt restraints). r In penetrating trauma, note the characteristic of the weapon (type and caliber), distance from the weapon, or the type and length of knife or impaling object: – Injuries result from a combination of the kinetic energy and shear forces of penetration. Physical Examr Systemic signs from acute blood loss: – Syncope, dizziness, weakness, confusion – Hypotension or shock r Local signs: – LUQ abdominal tenderness – Palpable tender mass in LUQ (Balance sign) – Referred pain to the left shoulder (Kehr sign) – Abdominal distention, rigidity, rebound tenderness, involuntary guarding r Contusions, abrasions, or penetrating wounds to the chest, flank, or abdomen may indicate underlying spleen injury

It is 2–4 times more common in males. – Of those with spondylolysis, 50% will have some degree of spondylolisthesis develop during their lifetime, and 50% of those will be symptomatic: – Literature does not associate athletic activity with increased slippage. – Spondylolisthesis predisposes to nerve root impingement and frequently sciatica. r Classification: – Type 1—dysplastic: Congenital defect of the neural arch or intra-articular facets is often associated with spina bifida occulta – Type 2—isthmic: Stress fracture from repetitive microtrauma through the neural arch – Type 3—degenerative: Long-standing segmental instability – Type 4—traumatic – Type 5—pathologic: Generalized or focal bone disease – Spondylolisthesis is divided into 4 grades based on degree of slippage (Meyerding gr
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr Onset often gradual, unless traumatic r Often associated with feeling of stiffness or spasm in paravertebral muscles r Pain in the back and proximal legs aggravated by standing and walking r Sitting or forward bending relieves pain. r Pain occurs after varying amounts of exercise, with standing, or with coughing: – Aggravating factors can include repetitive hyperextending movements. – Alleviating factors can include rest, although the course is variable and slow and usually requires sitting or stooping positions. r Systemic/neurologic symptoms: Minimal, unless there is significant trauma or “slip.” Physical Examr Hyperlordotic posture: – Trunk may appear shortened. – Rib cage approaches iliac crests. r Hamstring tightness: – Knees flexed to allow patient to stand upright r Only “typical” finding is 1-legged hyperextension: – Standing on 1 leg and leaning backward reproduces pain on ipsilateral side. r Palpation may reveal step-off with a prominent spinous p
management: management decisions through identification of new stress fractures and healing of old stress fractures. – If a CT scan is obtained in the ED, sagittal reconstructions should be performed and the CT scanner should be at minimum a 16-slice scanner. – Outpatient evaluation unless history of recent trauma. r MRI—exact role not yet clarified in literature: – Useful for defining nerve root impingement and central canal and neuroforaminal narrowing. – May be useful in the assessment of acuity of abnormality. – Can identify alternate pathologic diagnoses. Carter BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Sternoclavicular joint (SCJ) is the only joint that connects the upper limb to the trunk. r Among the least frequently injured joints in the body r Most commonly due to athletic or vehicular injuries r Congenital or spontaneous dislocation and subluxation are rarely seen r SCJ stability depends on ligamentous attachments, primarily anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments, interclavicular ligament, and costoclavicular ligament ETIOLOGYr Injury to the SCJ can be from sprains, subluxations, or dislocations of the ligamentous structure r In sprains, ligamentous capsule remains intact r Subluxation occurs when sternoclavicular ligament ruptures while costoclavicular ligament remains intact r Complete ligamentous disruption leads to dislocation r The SCJ can dislocate anteriorly or posteriorly. A large force is required. A greater force is required to displace the clavicle posteriorly. r Direction of dislocation depends on the shoulder position: – Anterior dislocation more likely when the acromion is posterior to the manubrium. – Posterior dislocation more likely when the acromion is anterior to the manubrium. r Anterior dislocation is more common (more than 90% of dislocation

Sloane BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Tasers are part of a class of less lethal weapons referred to as conducted energy weapons (CEWs). r Most common in US are those made by Taser International; these include the M-26, X-26, and X2 although others exist. r These devices use a high-voltage low-amperage current to override the subject’s ability to control the peripheral nervous system; they cause pain so as to induce subject compliance. r Handheld devices such as stun guns require the application of 2 exposed probes to the skin (or close to the skin) to cause a localized response (usually pain). r Other devices, such as the Taser International devices, have barbed probes attached to thin wires that can be shot up to 35 ft to deliver current from a distance. r Needle lengths of CEW barbs are of varied lengths but generally less than or around 0.5 in. r The effects of CEWs vary depending on the type of device being used, location, placement, and distance between the probes on the subject’s body. management: TREATMENT PRE-HOSPITALr There is no definitive treatment that can be rendered in the field. r Pre-hospital personnel must recognize the urgency of acute testicular pain in young patients. r These patients should be transported to the ED immediately. INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY IV fluid, analgesics as appropriate ED TREATMENT/PROCEDURESr Rapid triage and assessment r Exam of testicle to exclude primary neoplasm r Establish the diagnosis and mobilize appropriate urologic care. r Applying an ice pack to the scrotum relieves pain: – May prolong the viability of the ischemic testicle r If definitive care is likely to be delayed beyond 4–5 hr from the onset of torsion, manual detorsion may be attempted (26.5–80% successful). – Externally rotate the affected testicle opposite the usual medial direction of torsion. – Continue until pain is relieved, normal anatomy is restored, or Doppler US shows return of flow. – All patients who undergo manual detorsion must be surgically explored. Oyama BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Distal phalangeal fractures: – Blunt trauma, hyperextension of the thumb, axial loading of the thumb, and crush injuries. – Tuft fracture is a similar fracture in other digits, in which the distal phalanx is crushed and/or fragmented. – It may be open or closed and associated with nail bed injury. – Severe nail bed injury, intra-articular, displaced/angulated fractures, or tendon injuries warrant orthopedics’ consultation. – Noncomplex tuft fractures can be splinted and treated as soft tissue injuries. r Proximal phalangeal fractures and thumb metacarpal fractures: – Blunt trauma to the thumb: ◦Axial loading of the thumb with the metacarpophalangeal (MP) joint partially flexed, the hand closed or the thumb MP joint otherwise stabilized – Bennett fracture (type I): ◦Intra-articular fracture/dislocation at the base of the metacarpal where the ulnar aspect of the metacarpal maintains its attachment. – Rolando fracture (type II): ◦Comminuted Y- or T-shaped intra-articular fracture of the base of the 1st metacarpal. ◦Similar to a comminuted Bennett, these can be much more complex with multiple comminuted fractures. – Type III fractures ◦Extra-articular metacarpal fractures. Edlow BASICS DESCRIPTION Even in high endemic areas for tick-borne diseases, the risk of infection with a tick-borne pathogen is very low. After a tick bite, patient concerns include: r Tick removal r Local effect of the bite r Possibility of acquiring a tick-borne illness: – Fear of contracting Lyme disease – Desire to be tested or treated for Lyme ETIOLOGYr Specific tick-borne infections are discussed in other chapters. r Tick bite can be from different species of ticks of 2 major types: – Soft ticks (Ornithodoros): ◦Cause tick-borne relapsing fever ◦Only feed for minutes and therefore almost never provoke a visit to the ED – Hard ticks—especially Ixodes and Dermacentor: ◦Feed for several days to a week and therefore, more likely to be noticed by patient and lead to an ED visit r Lyme disease transmission: – Species of tick, stage of development, duration of attachment, and geography may all play a role in the possibility of developing Lyme disease. – Most cases of Lyme are associated with bites from nymphal Ixodes scapularis ticks. – Most cases of Lyme are transmitted only after the tick has been attached for 24–48 hr: ◦Degree of engorgement is a marker for duration of attachment. DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Tick is attached to skin. Historyr Th
diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Tick is attached to skin. Historyr The patient usually has made the diagnosis themselves, although sometimes they mistake the tick for skin tags or other skin lesions. r Ask regarding duration of tick attachment, as this may influence the decision to prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis. Physical Exam Directly examine the skin and the tick: r Try to identify the tick species. r Estimate degree of engorgement. ALERT r Some tick-borne infections are potentially fatal. Because there are no confirmatory diagnostic tests that are available in real time, they must be diagnosed based on history, physical, and epidemiologic context. r Because the drug of choice for some of these infections—doxycycline—is not usually prescribed for empiric therapy for acutely ill febrile patients, ask about the potential for tick bites in the history of febrile patients and consider using this drug in the appropriate settings. highYieldSummary: P1: OSO/OVY P2: OSO/OVY QC: OSO/OVY T1: OSO LWBK1336-driver-V LWBK1336-Schaider ch602.xml May 16, 2014 18:55 VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY Cameron R. Wangsgard rBo E. Madsen BASICS DESCRIPTIONr Inadequacy of the venous valves that causes impaired venous drainage leading to edema of the lower extremities. r A chronic condition of lower extremity vascular incompetence. r Normal blood flow in the venous system is unidirectional from the superficial veins to the deep veins. r Unidirectional flow is maintained by contraction of leg muscles and by valves within the veins. r Damage to the valves, e.g. following DVT, causes them to become rigid and they lose their ability to prevent retrograde blood flow properly. r Decreased venous return from lower extremities causes increased pressure and distention of the veins, which in turn causes separation of the valve leaflets. r Increased pressure transmitted into the dermal microcirculation results in extravasation of macromolecules and red blood cells causing inflammatory injury resulting in ulcer formation, skin changes, and poor ulcer healing. diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMS Historyr Asymptomatic phase: – Venous dilation ranging from venous flares to small varicosities r Symptomatic phase: – Ankle and calf swelling – Varicose veins – Skin discoloration/hyperpigmentation – Ulcer formation – Lipodermatosclerosis – Dull ache/pain in the legs: ◦Worsened by prolonged standing ◦Resolves with leg elevation – Burning sensation – Pruritus – Night cramps Physical Examr Varicose veins r Ankle- and calf-dependent edema r Ulcers, most often situated over the malleoli or medial portion of calf: – Must have preserved peripheral pulses to ensure ulcers are due to venous insufficiency and not arterial insufficiency r Red, purple discoloration of skin r Telangiectasias r Reticular veins r Stasis dermatitis r Brownish hyperpigmentation r Sclerosis, induration, and atrophy of skin r Bacterial infection: – Surrounding cellulitis – Rapidly growing ulcer – Purulent drainage from ulcer – Increased pain – Fever – Lymphangitis r Other etiologies than venous insu

diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS SIGNS AND SYMPTOMSr Loss of consciousness r Seizure r Transient gasping followed by apnea r Absent pulse and heart sounds r Death if the rhythm remains untreated: – VF is the initial rhythm in ∼5–70% of patients sustaining sudden cardiac death in the pre-hospital setting ESSENTIAL WORKUPr AED or manual defibrillator to confirm and treat a shockable rhythm r Cardiac monitor DIAGNOSIS TESTS & INTERPRETATION Labr Lab tests are not useful during resuscitation r After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC): Electrolytes including calcium and magnesium, BUN, creatinine, troponin, ABG, lactic acid level, and toxicology screen Imagingr After ROSC r To identify cause of VF: – EKG – Cardiac US – CXR, also to monitor placement of an endotracheal tube (ETT) DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSISr Asystole: – Fine VF may mimic asystole in a single lead. – Check rhythm in another lead for fine fibrillations TREATMENT ALERT r Early defibrillation of VF is the most important determinant of survival, and each minut

INITIAL STABILIZATION/THERAPY Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation. Secure adequate IV access.
